citations.quote:
Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

For the seminorms of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]], a basic neighbourhood of $f_0\in\mathcal S$ is
$$\{f:p_{\alpha_r\beta_r}(f-f_0)<\varepsilon_r\ (1\le r\le m)\},\qquad m<\infty,\quad\varepsilon_r>0.$$
The empty intersection is the whole space. The topology consists of unions of these neighbourhoods. A sequence $f_k$ converges to $f$ precisely when $p_{\alpha\beta}(f_k-f)\to0$ for every pair of multi-indices: necessity follows from the one-condition neighbourhoods, and sufficiency follows by taking the maximum of the finitely many convergence thresholds in a basic neighbourhood.

A complex topological vector space is called locally convex here when zero has a base of convex balanced sets; balanced means $|c|\le1$ implies $cV\subseteq V$. The displayed sets about zero are convex and balanced by the seminorm inequalities. They also show addition is continuous, by halving each tolerance. Scalar multiplication is jointly continuous: near $(c_0,f_0)$, restrict $|c-c_0|<1$ and use
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(cf-c_0f_0)\le (|c_0|+1)p_{\alpha\beta}(f-f_0)+|c-c_0|p_{\alpha\beta}(f_0).$$
There are finitely many bounds to enforce. Finally $p_{00}(f-g)>0$ for distinct functions; balls of radius less than half this number separate them. Thus this is a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space. All these verifications use only finite choices.

Fix an integer $n\geq1$.  A **tempered distribution** on $\mathbb R^n$ is a
continuous complex-linear functional

$$u:\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow\mathbb C,$$

where Schwartz space and its locally convex topology are those of
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]] and
[[def-schwartz-topology-and-convergence]].  The space of all such functionals
is denoted $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.

We write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$.  This pairing is bilinear:
the test variable is not conjugated.  Thus $u(a\varphi+b\psi)=
a\langle u,\varphi\rangle+b\langle u,\psi\rangle$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C$.
The zero functional is tempered.  Continuity is topological continuity, and,
because the Schwartz topology is generated by a countable cofinal family of
seminorms, it is equivalently continuity on every convergent sequence.  No
choice principle is used in this definition.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

For integers $p,q\ge 1$ and open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, $V\subseteq\mathbb R^q$, every $\Phi\in\mathcal D(U\times V)$ is a limit in the LF test topology of finite sums of products $f(x)g(y)$ with $f\in\mathcal D(U)$ and $g\in\mathcal D(V)$. All approximating supports and the target support lie in one compact product inside $U\times V$. This holds in ZF.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $v\in\mathcal D'(V)$ the tensor candidate is a distribution on $U\times V$, uniquely determined by $(u\otimes v)(\varphi\otimes\psi)=u(\varphi)v(\psi)$. Its two iterated pairing orders agree, and $\operatorname{supp}(u\otimes v)=\operatorname{supp}u\times\operatorname{supp}v$. Three-factor pairings associate. Moreover $\partial_x^\alpha(u\otimes v)=(\partial^\alpha u)\otimes v$ and $\partial_y^\beta(u\otimes v)=u\otimes(\partial^\beta v)$. All claims hold in ZF.

derivations.claim: By continuity [F3], there is a basic neighbourhood $V_u$ of zero such that $|u(f)|<1$ on $V_u$. Write $V_u=\{f:p_{\alpha_j\beta_j}(f)<\varepsilon_j,\ 1\le j\le k\}$ using [F2], and let $M_u$ be the largest component of these finitely many multi-indices. Put $P_{M_u}(f)=\max_{|\alpha|,|\beta|\le M_u}p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$ and $c_u=2\max_j\varepsilon_j^{-1}$. If $P_{M_u}(f)>0$, then $f/(2\max_j(p_{\alpha_j\beta_j}(f)/\varepsilon_j))\in V_u$, so linearity gives $|u(f)|\le c_uP_{M_u}(f)$. If the denominator vanishes, every positive scalar multiple of $f$ lies in $V_u$, forcing $u(f)=0$ and the same bound. The same argument gives $|v(g)|\le c_vP_{M_v}(g)$ for some finite $M_v,c_v$.

For fixed $\Phi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{p+q})$, the map $x\mapsto\Phi(x,\cdot)$ is smooth with values in $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^q)$: Taylor's formula in the $x$ coordinates, with its remainder differentiated in $y$, tends to zero in each $p_{\gamma\delta}$ on every compact $x$ set because every mixed Schwartz seminorm of $\Phi$ is finite. Continuity of $v$ therefore makes $h(x):=v(\Phi(x,\cdot))$ smooth and gives $\partial_x^\beta h(x)=v(\partial_x^\beta\Phi(x,\cdot))$. For every $\alpha,\beta$, [F3] and step 1.1 yield $\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial_x^\beta h(x)|\le c_v\max_{|\gamma|,|\delta|\le M_v}\sup_{x,y}|x^\alpha y^\gamma\partial_x^\beta\partial_y^\delta\Phi(x,y)|<\infty.$ Thus $h\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^p)$.

Define $w(\Phi)=u(h)$. Applying the bound in step 1.1 to the finitely many $x$ seminorms with indices at most $M_u$, and then the displayed estimate in step 2.1, bounds $|w(\Phi)|$ by a finite constant times the maximum of finitely many product Schwartz seminorms of $\Phi$. Hence $w$ is continuous on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{p+q})$. For $\Phi=\varphi\otimes\psi$, the inner pairing is $\varphi(x)v(\psi)$, giving the claimed product value; on compactly supported tests the formula is the same iterated pairing as [F6].

Finite sums of Schwartz product tests are dense in $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{p+q})$. Indeed, choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^p)$ and $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^q)$ equal to one near the unit balls by [F4], and set $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ and $\eta_R(y)=\eta(y/R)$. The product rule and rapid decay show $\chi_R(x)\eta_R(y)\Phi(x,y)\to\Phi(x,y)$ in every product Schwartz seminorm: the undifferentiated tails lie outside balls of radius proportional to $R$, and each differentiated cutoff contributes a factor $R^{-j}$ on the same tails. For fixed $R$, [F5] approximates this compactly supported smooth function by finite sums of product tests with common compact support; on that support, uniform convergence of all derivatives implies convergence in every Schwartz seminorm. Thus any two continuous functionals with the same product values agree on a dense subspace and hence everywhere. The same density argument, iterated over finitely many factors, shows that different parenthesizations of the constructed tensor product agree; this also agrees with the compact-test associativity in [F6].

definition_review.statement: Defines the dimension-indexed tempered hierarchy, algebra and involutions, distinct ordinary/reflection positivity forms, nonempty directed regulator data, fixed-order convergence, continuity records, an explicit non-OS-equivalent illustrative order bound, Euclidean invariance, permutation symmetry, and clustering.
definition_review.edge_cases: The definition explicitly covers d=1, n=0, zero higher moments, strict positive time, empty endpoint cases, and nonempty regulator sets.

derivations.claim: For each $n\ge1$, define the product-test map $J_n:S_d^{\otimes_{\rm alg}n}\to S_{d,n}$ by $J_n(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)$ and linear extension; the product of Schwartz functions is a Schwartz function. Set $J_0(c)=c$ and, for $a\in T_d$, define $Q_S(a):=\omega_S(\Theta a\,a)$. Fix a finite positive-time polynomial $a=\sum_{j=0}^{N}a_j$, with each $a_j$ a finite sum of degree-$j$ product tests. Expanding concatenation and the moment functional gives the finite sum $Q_{S^\lambda}(a)=\sum_{j,k=0}^{N}\langle S^\lambda_{j+k},J_{j+k}((\Theta a_j)a_k)\rangle .$ Every test in this finite sum is fixed independently of $\lambda$, so [A2] gives $Q_{S^\lambda}(a)\to Q_S(a)$. By [A1], every value $Q_{S^\lambda}(a)$ is a nonnegative real number. Since $[0,\infty)$ is closed in $\mathbb C$, its limit $Q_S(a)$ is also a nonnegative real number. As $a$ was arbitrary, $S$ is reflection positive.

Fix one Euclidean isometry $\gamma(x)=Rx+b$ and one order-$n$ test $\Phi$. The pullback $\Phi\mapsto\Phi\circ(\gamma^{-1})^{\times n}$ is continuous on Schwartz space: the chain rule writes each derivative as a finite linear combination of derivatives of $\Phi$ evaluated at the inverse affine image, and each polynomial weight in $x$ becomes a finite sum of polynomial weights in the new variable with fixed coefficients. Thus each transformed Schwartz seminorm is bounded by finitely many original seminorms. If every $S^\lambda_n$ is invariant under this fixed pullback, [A2] applied to both $\Phi$ and its pullback passes the equality to $S_n$. A permutation of argument blocks is a coordinate permutation and preserves the same seminorms exactly, so the same limit argument passes permutation symmetry. Step 1.1 uses only a fixed finite number of orders and tests; it supplies neither a uniform-in-$n$ bound nor a limit as a translation parameter tends to infinity, so it proves no order-uniform growth or clustering claim.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, write Euclidean space as $E_d=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{d-1}$ with coordinates $x=(t,\mathbf x)$, and put $S_d=\mathcal S(E_d;\mathbb C)$ and $S_{d,n}=\mathcal S(E_d^n;\mathbb C)$ for $n\ge1$, with $S_{d,0}=\mathbb C$. For $d=1$, $\mathbb R^0$ is the one-point vector space with unit measure. A Schwinger hierarchy is a sequence $S=(S_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $S_0=1$ and each $S_n\in S_{d,n}'$; its moments on elementary tests are $\langle S_n,f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n\rangle$. The associated unital algebraic test algebra is $T_d=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}^{\rm alg}S_d^{\otimes_{\rm alg}n}$ with concatenation multiplication, unit $1\in S_{d,0}=\mathbb C$, and involution $(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)^*=\overline f_n\otimes\cdots\otimes\overline f_1$ and $(c1)^*=\overline c1$. The moments define $\omega_S:T_d\to\mathbb C$ by linear extension. At $d=4$ this is the same four-dimensional algebra and moment convention used by the positive-tempered-moment definition.

Ordinary moment positivity means $\omega_S(1)=1$ and $\omega_S(a^*a)\ge0$ for every $a\in T_d$. It is distinct from reflection positivity. Let $\vartheta(t,\mathbf x)=(-t,\mathbf x)$ and $E_{d,+}=\{(t,\mathbf x):t>0\}$. The positive-time polynomial algebra $T_{d,+}$ is the unital star subalgebra generated by tests in $C_c^\infty(E_{d,+};\mathbb C)$. Define the antilinear reflection $\Theta$ by $\Theta f=\overline{f\circ\vartheta}$ on degree one, $\Theta(c1)=\overline c1$, and $\Theta(ab)=\Theta(b)\Theta(a)$. Reflection positivity is $\omega_S(\Theta a\,a)\in[0,\infty)$ for every $a\in T_{d,+}$. The same formula applies to finite-site test algebras with an involution exchanging the sites.

A regulated hierarchy is a family $S^\lambda=(S^\lambda_n)_{n\ge0}$ indexed by a nonempty directed set $(\Lambda,\preceq)$, where directed means every two indices have a common upper bound. A distributional continuum limit is a hierarchy $S$ such that for every fixed $n$ and every $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$, $\langle S^\lambda_n,\Phi\rangle\to\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle$ as $\lambda$ advances in $\Lambda$. A limit contract records these pairings, the regulator family, and any additional uniform estimates; pointwise-in-$n$ convergence by itself asserts no uniform bound as $n$ varies.

For explicit comparison, define the Schwartz seminorm $P_k(\Phi)=\max_{|\alpha|,|\beta|\le k}\sup_{x\in E_d^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta\Phi(x)|$ on $S_{d,n}$. A per-order uniform continuity record is a choice, for each fixed $n$, of $r_n\in\mathbb N_0$ and $C_n\ge0$ such that $|\langle S^\lambda_n,\Phi\rangle|\le C_nP_{r_n}(\Phi)$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. A uniform-order bound is the stronger explicit condition that there exist fixed $s\in\mathbb N$ and $A,B,q>0$ with $|\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle|\le A B^n(n!)^q P_{sn}(\Phi)$ for every $n\ge1$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. This bound is recorded separately and is not inferred from distributional convergence or asserted equivalent to a corrected Osterwalder–Schrader regularity hypothesis.

For $\gamma(x)=Rx+a$ with $R\in O(d)$ and $a\in E_d$, define $(U_\gamma\Phi)(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\Phi(\gamma^{-1}x_1,\ldots,\gamma^{-1}x_n)$. Euclidean invariance means $\langle S_n,U_\gamma\Phi\rangle=\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle$ for every such $\gamma$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. Permutation symmetry means invariance of the pairing under each permutation of its $n$ argument blocks. Clustering means that for every $n,m\ge1$, $f\in S_{d,n}$ and $g\in S_{d,m}$,

$$
\langle S_{n+m},f\otimes\tau_{ae_0}g\rangle\longrightarrow \langle S_n,f\rangle\langle S_m,g\rangle\quad(a\to+\infty),
$$

where $e_0=(1,\mathbf0)$ and $(\tau_{ae_0}g)(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=g(x_1-ae_0,\ldots,x_m-ae_0)$. This contract definition asserts neither existence of a regulated limit nor any of these additional properties.

Let $p,q\ge1$, let $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^p)$ and $v\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^q)$, and use the Schwartz seminorms $p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$. The iterated pairing

$$
w(\Phi):=u\!\left(x\mapsto v\!\left(y\mapsto\Phi(x,y)\right)\right),\qquad \Phi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{p+q}),
$$

defines a tempered distribution $w\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^{p+q})$. It satisfies $w(\varphi\otimes\psi)=u(\varphi)v(\psi)$ for Schwartz functions $\varphi,\psi$. It agrees with the distribution tensor product on compactly supported tests, is unique with these product values, and its finite iterates are associative.

Use the Schwartz spaces and their seminorm topologies of
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]] and
[[def-schwartz-topology-and-convergence]]. Put
$S:=\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C)$ and
$S_n:=\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{4n};\mathbb C)$ for $n\ge1$, and set
$S_0:=\mathbb C$. A tempered distribution in $S_n'$ means a continuous
complex-linear functional on $S_n$
as in [[def-tempered-distribution]]; its pairing with a test is bilinear.

For complex vector spaces $S$, let $S^{\otimes_{\rm alg} n}$ be the algebraic
tensor product, characterized by multilinear maps out of $S^n$, with
$S^{\otimes_{\rm alg}0}:=\mathbb C1$. Define the algebraic tensor test algebra
$$T(S):=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}^{\rm alg}S^{\otimes_{\rm alg}n},$$
where the direct sum consists of finite-support sequences. Its multiplication
is concatenation of tensor factors, extended bilinearly, and its unit is $1$
in degree zero. Its conjugate-linear involution is specified on elementary
tensors by
$$(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)^*:=\overline{f_n}\otimes\cdots\otimes\overline{f_1},\qquad (c1)^*=\overline c1.$$

For $f_j\in S$, the elementary tensor is evaluated against a distribution by
the test function
$$J_n(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\prod_{j=1}^n f_j(x_j).$$
This is in $S_n$: for multi-indices split into four-coordinate blocks
$(\alpha_j,\beta_j)$, its Schwartz seminorm is
$$p_{(\alpha_j)_j,(\beta_j)_j}(J_n(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n))=\prod_{j=1}^n p_{\alpha_j\beta_j}(f_j).$$
Thus $J_n$ is multilinear and continuous, and the displayed formula extends
linearly to the algebraic tensor product.
In degree zero set $J_0(c1):=c$.

By these definitions concatenation is associative with the degree-zero unit,
and reversal together with complex conjugation is an involution satisfying
$(ab)^*=b^*a^*$; thus $T(S)$ is a unital complex star algebra.

A **positive tempered moment family** is a sequence consisting of $W_0=1$
and $W_n\in S_n'$ for each $n\ge1$ such that the multilinear maps
$$f_1,\ldots,f_n\longmapsto\langle W_n,J_n(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)\rangle$$
extend, degree by degree and then over finite sums, to a complex-linear
functional $\omega:T(S)\to\mathbb C$ satisfying
$$\omega(1)=1,\qquad \omega(a^*a)\in[0,\infty)\quad(a\in T(S)).$$
Equivalently, the family supplies an actually positive normalized functional
on this algebra. Positivity is a hypothesis on the distributions; formal
coefficient families do not qualify merely because they obey algebraic
identities. No topology on $T(S)$, norm completion, C*-algebra, or existence
claim for an interacting field is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite and let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ matrix; positive-semidefinite means $u^{\mathsf T}Cu\ge0$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^N$. The centered multivariate normal Borel probability law with covariance $C$ is $\gamma_C:=N_N(0,C)$ as defined by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: every linear projection $q\mapsto u^{\mathsf T}q$ has scalar normal law $N(0,u^{\mathsf T}Cu)$, and the law exists even when $C$ is singular. Here $N(0,\sigma^2)$ is the law specified in [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], with density $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for the standard case.

Let $U:\mathbb R^N\to[0,\infty)$ be a real homogeneous quartic polynomial, meaning $U$ is a polynomial and $U(sq)=s^4U(q)$ for all $s\in\mathbb R$ and $q\in\mathbb R^N$. For a coupling $\lambda\ge0$, define the partition integral and its weighted measure by

$$Z_{C,U}(\lambda):=\int_{\mathbb R^N}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q),\qquad \nu_{C,U,\lambda}(A):=\int_Ae^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q)$$

for Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^N$. Whenever $0<Z_{C,U}(\lambda)<\infty$, the **finite Euclidean interacting measure** is the Borel probability measure

$$d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}(q):=Z_{C,U}(\lambda)^{-1}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q).$$

For a polynomial $P:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R$ with finite integral, write $\langle P\rangle_{C,U,\lambda}:=\int P\,d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}$. The exact supplier [[thm-qft-finite-euclidean-polynomial-measure]] proves that $Z_{C,U}(\lambda)$ is positive and finite and that every polynomial insertion is integrable. This is a Borel measure on finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^N$; it is not a measure on distributions on continuum Euclidean spacetime and does not by itself assert reflection positivity or reconstruction of a continuum field.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite, let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ covariance matrix, and let $Q\sim\gamma_C=N_N(0,C)$ be the law of [[def-qft-finite-euclidean-interacting-measure]]. For $k\ge0$ and vectors $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in\mathbb R^N$, every product $\prod_{j=1}^k(u_j^{\mathsf T}Q)$ is integrable. For $k=0$ its expectation is $1$. If $k$ is odd, its expectation is $0$; if $k=2m$, then

$$\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^{2m}u_j^{\mathsf T}Q\right]=\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Pair}(2m)}\prod_{\{a,b\}\in\pi}u_a^{\mathsf T}Cu_b,$$

where $\operatorname{Pair}(2m)$ is the finite set of partitions of $\{1,\ldots,2m\}$ into unordered two-element subsets. Thus every real polynomial $P$ in $Q$ satisfies $\mathbb E|P(Q)|<\infty$, and its expectation $\mathbb E[P(Q)]$ is computed by expanding $P$ into monomials and applying finitely many covariance pairings.

Assume [[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]], exactly as required by the
published Schwartz Fourier theorem.  For $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$
put

$$\widehat\varphi(\xi)=\mathcal F\varphi(\xi) =\int_{\mathbb R^n}\varphi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$

For $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ define its **Fourier transform** by

$$\langle\mathcal Fu,\varphi\rangle =\langle u,\mathcal F\varphi\rangle \qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)).$$

The published automorphism
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]]
sends Schwartz tests continuously to Schwartz tests, so composition with the
continuous functional of [[def-tempered-distribution]] is again a continuous
complex-linear functional.  Hence $\mathcal Fu\in\mathcal S'$.  The pairing
is bilinear: there is no conjugation and no inverse transform on the
right-hand side.  Countable Choice is used only through the cited published
Fourier construction; transposition itself uses no additional choice.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim: The full Axiom of Choice assumed in [A1] implies Countable Choice: if $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is any sequence of nonempty sets, AC supplies a choice function $g$ on the family $\{X_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$, and $n\mapsto g(X_n)$ chooses from every $X_n$. Thus the actual Countable Choice hypotheses of [F6] and [F7] are satisfied before those suppliers are used. The full Fourier transform $\widehat\Phi$ of $\Phi\in\mathcal S(E_d\times E_d)$ is Schwartz by [F6]. For $|p|\ge1$, some coordinate $p_j$ satisfies $|p_j|\ge |p|/\sqrt d$; the monomial-weight seminorm $P_N$ includes the weight given by the $N$th power of that coordinate in the first Fourier block. For $|p|<1$, its zero-weight seminorm bounds the value. Thus, with the finite dimension/order constant $K_{d,N}:=2^N d^{N/2}$, $$|\widehat\Phi(-p,p)|\le K_{d,N}P_N(\widehat\Phi)(1+|p|)^{-N}.$$ For an integer $N>d$, this proves absolute convergence and bounds the defining pairing by $(2\pi)^{-d}m^{-2}K_{d,N}P_N(\widehat\Phi)\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+|p|)^{-N}\,dp$. The last integral is finite: dyadic annuli have volume $O(2^{jd})$ while the integrand is $O(2^{-jN})$. Fourier continuity in [F6] bounds $P_N(\widehat\Phi)$ by finitely many Schwartz seminorms of $\Phi$, so $C_m^{(2)}$ is continuous and tempered. Under simultaneous translation by $a\in E_d$, the full Fourier transform acquires the factor $e^{-i(q_1+q_2)\cdot a}$; at $(q_1,q_2)=(-p,p)$ this factor is $1$, proving translation invariance. On product tests, $C_m(\bar f,g)=(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\frac{\overline{\widehat f(p)}\,\widehat g(p)}{p_0^2+|\mathbf k|^2+m^2}\,dp,$ which is nonnegative for $g=f$.

The zeroth term $S_0=1$ is a continuous functional on $\mathbb C$, and every odd-order term $S_n=0$ is the zero continuous functional. citations.quote:
Fix an integer $d\ge1$, write Euclidean space as $E_d=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{d-1}$ with coordinates $x=(t,\mathbf x)$, and put $S_d=\mathcal S(E_d;\mathbb C)$ and $S_{d,n}=\mathcal S(E_d^n;\mathbb C)$ for $n\ge1$, with $S_{d,0}=\mathbb C$. For $d=1$, $\mathbb R^0$ is the one-point vector space with unit measure. A Schwinger hierarchy is a sequence $S=(S_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $S_0=1$ and each $S_n\in S_{d,n}'$; its moments on elementary tests are $\langle S_n,f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n\rangle$. The associated unital algebraic test algebra is $T_d=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}^{\rm alg}S_d^{\otimes_{\rm alg}n}$ with concatenation multiplication, unit $1\in S_{d,0}=\mathbb C$, and involution $(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)^*=\overline f_n\otimes\cdots\otimes\overline f_1$ and $(c1)^*=\overline c1$. The moments define $\omega_S:T_d\to\mathbb C$ by linear extension. At $d=4$ this is the same four-dimensional algebra and moment convention used by the positive-tempered-moment definition.

Ordinary moment positivity means $\omega_S(1)=1$ and $\omega_S(a^*a)\ge0$ for every $a\in T_d$. It is distinct from reflection positivity. Let $\vartheta(t,\mathbf x)=(-t,\mathbf x)$ and $E_{d,+}=\{(t,\mathbf x):t>0\}$. The positive-time polynomial algebra $T_{d,+}$ is the unital star subalgebra generated by tests in $C_c^\infty(E_{d,+};\mathbb C)$. Define the antilinear reflection $\Theta$ by $\Theta f=\overline{f\circ\vartheta}$ on degree one, $\Theta(c1)=\overline c1$, and $\Theta(ab)=\Theta(b)\Theta(a)$. Reflection positivity is $\omega_S(\Theta a\,a)\in[0,\infty)$ for every $a\in T_{d,+}$. The same formula applies to finite-site test algebras with an involution exchanging the sites.

A regulated hierarchy is a family $S^\lambda=(S^\lambda_n)_{n\ge0}$ indexed by a nonempty directed set $(\Lambda,\preceq)$, where directed means every two indices have a common upper bound. A distributional continuum limit is a hierarchy $S$ such that for every fixed $n$ and every $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$, $\langle S^\lambda_n,\Phi\rangle\to\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle$ as $\lambda$ advances in $\Lambda$. A limit contract records these pairings, the regulator family, and any additional uniform estimates; pointwise-in-$n$ convergence by itself asserts no uniform bound as $n$ varies.

For explicit comparison, define the Schwartz seminorm $P_k(\Phi)=\max_{|\alpha|,|\beta|\le k}\sup_{x\in E_d^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta\Phi(x)|$ on $S_{d,n}$. A per-order uniform continuity record is a choice, for each fixed $n$, of $r_n\in\mathbb N_0$ and $C_n\ge0$ such that $|\langle S^\lambda_n,\Phi\rangle|\le C_nP_{r_n}(\Phi)$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. A uniform-order bound is the stronger explicit condition that there exist fixed $s\in\mathbb N$ and $A,B,q>0$ with $|\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle|\le A B^n(n!)^q P_{sn}(\Phi)$ for every $n\ge1$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. This bound is recorded separately and is not inferred from distributional convergence or asserted equivalent to a corrected Osterwalder–Schrader regularity hypothesis.

For $\gamma(x)=Rx+a$ with $R\in O(d)$ and $a\in E_d$, define $(U_\gamma\Phi)(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\Phi(\gamma^{-1}x_1,\ldots,\gamma^{-1}x_n)$. Euclidean invariance means $\langle S_n,U_\gamma\Phi\rangle=\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle$ for every such $\gamma$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. Permutation symmetry means invariance of the pairing under each permutation of its $n$ argument blocks. Clustering means that for every $n,m\ge1$, $f\in S_{d,n}$ and $g\in S_{d,m}$,

$$
\langle S_{n+m},f\otimes\tau_{ae_0}g\rangle\longrightarrow \langle S_n,f\rangle\langle S_m,g\rangle\quad(a\to+\infty),
$$

where $e_0=(1,\mathbf0)$ and $(\tau_{ae_0}g)(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=g(x_1-ae_0,\ldots,x_m-ae_0)$. This contract definition asserts neither existence of a regulated limit nor any of these additional properties.

derivations.claim: All four weights are positive and sum to $(1-r)/2+(1+r)/2=1$. Symmetry of the support weights gives $\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[Y]=0$, and $X^2=Y^2=1$ at every support point, so the covariance diagonal is $(1,1)$. The equal-sign outcomes have total probability $(1-r)/2$ and product $XY=1$; the opposite-sign outcomes have total probability $(1+r)/2$ and product $XY=-1$. Therefore $\mathbb E[XY]=(1-r)/2-(1+r)/2=-r$.

The covariance matrix is $C=\begin{pmatrix}1&-r\\-r&1\end{pmatrix}$. For real $u,v$, $(u,v)C(u,v)^{\mathsf T}=(u-rv)^2+(1-r^2)v^2,$ which is strictly positive unless $(u,v)=(0,0)$ because $0<r<1$. Thus $C$ is positive definite and the probability law is ordinarily positive. Since $Y$ belongs to the declared positive-site algebra, take $F=Y$. Reflection positivity would require $\mathbb E[(\Theta F)F]=\mathbb E[XY]\ge0$, but this is $-r<0$. Hence the statement is false.
